notes: Eval 1 (create-order-service-method) is non-discriminating — both configurations passed 4/4. The baseline already knows the PDL pseudocode format well for a straightforward CRUD method. Consider replacing with a harder scenario that tests edge-case coverage more aggressively.

Eval 2 (validate-webhook-signature) is the strongest discriminator: with_skill 4/4, without_skill 0/4. The baseline skipped the pseudocode template entirely for a complex crypto middleware and went straight to implementation prose. The skill enforces the template even for hard cases.

Eval 3 (syntax-help-request) partially discriminates: with_skill 4/4, without_skill 2/4. The baseline failed the syntax-help assertions by refusing to show async/await and adding an unsolicited design question instead. Interestingly the baseline's refusal is arguably better pedagogically — but it violates the skill's explicit rule.
The without_skill baseline has high variance (stddev 0.47 pass_rate, stddev 17.5s time) — behavior is inconsistent across eval types, unlike with_skill which is perfectly consistent.

Token cost is comparable between configurations (~1400 more for with_skill) but time was actually faster with the skill for evals 1 and 3 — the skill's structure may reduce exploration time for simpler evals.

Key discriminator: whether Claude produces a structured pseudocode block at all (template with Purpose/In/Out/Edges) vs. jumping to implementation guidance. The skill reliably enforces this; the baseline does not for complex technical domains.
